  - heading "Why does my child know grammar rules but keep making mistakes?" [level=2]
  - text: It can be incredibly frustrating to hear your child repeat a mistake on a rule you
  - emphasis: know
  - text: they understand. However,
  - strong: knowing a grammar rule and executing it in real time are two entirely different brain functions
  - text: .
  - link "YouTube · English in Real Life_":
    - /url: /goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVwskNDZO7933iAVCR9bJpCucIQBX8-Mpv6p0d34euvnYRu_6szouy2Sp5vJSYmk0g19FZQ8-sm64WLNqiJ_gNkDkx9lzLcAN3azNznl_2fs3zwi-PS87uNg0T8_FS5X71EctWsw
  - button "YouTube · English in Real Life_ - Related results":
    - generic: YouTube
    - generic: ·English in Real Life_
  - text: When your child makes these errors, they aren't ignoring you or "forgetting" how to speak—their brain is simply navigating the complex mechanics of language processing.
  - link "Quora":
    - /url: /goto?url=CAESnAEB6zswFYsSZtQb7P20EU2NPZxUkAtoaAoluxhw-J6L0RwP7pWaAY7irjSGvSShJ4cm73-aguZSC_SQDlm4kLOCD7gG26_24HmTcPFhSSBP8dPQQrelSTPeRm1BF54y4HGp9izMzxzbQYcCLf6vUPP-qxkvRzOI2mYWqF2swBlUuCkzMx6A8maDLfZ1z_3JxIOt7nrk4cBn-1k3Wb8

  - heading "1. High Cognitive Load (Brain Overload)" [level=3]
  - text: Studying grammar uses the conscious, analytical brain, but speaking or writing fluidly relies on the automatic, habitual brain. When children are in the middle of a real-time conversation or trying to draft an essay, they face a heavy
  - strong: cognitive load
  - text: . They are simultaneously balancing sentence structure, vocabulary choice, ideas, and tone. If they are excited, tired, or trying to articulate a complex thought, the brain falls back on its fastest, most ingrained habits or the easiest generalized rules just to keep up with the pace of thought.

  - heading "2. \"Overregularization\" (Computational Logic)" [level=3]
  - text: If your child used to say "went" perfectly but suddenly started saying
  - strong: "\"goed\" or \"runned,\""
  - text: they didn't actually regress. They are experiencing
  - strong: overregularization
  - text: .
  - link "Quora":
    - /url: /goto?url=CAESnAEB6zswFYsSZtQb7P20EU2NPZxUkAtoaAoluxhw-J6L0RwP7pWaAY7irjSGvSShJ4cm73-aguZSC_SQDlm4kLOCD7gG26_24HmTcPFhSSBP8dPQQrelSTPeRm1BF54y4HGp9izMzxzbQYcCLf6vUPP-qxkvRzOI2mYWqF2swBlUuCkzMx6A8maDLfZ1z_3JxIOt7nrk4cBn-1k3Wb8

  - list:

    - text: makes things past tense), it enthusiastically applies this algorithm to

  - heading "3. Theory vs. Application" [level=3]
  - text: Children often understand grammar rules abstractly (like filling out a worksheet) but struggle to bridge the gap into active production. A child might easily ace a punctuation test, but when writing a story, they fail to apply the rule because their focus has shifted from
  - emphasis: form
  - text: to
  - emphasis: content
  - text: .

  - list:
    - strong: "Use \"Modeling\" Instead of Direct Correction:"
    - text: Constantly stopping a child to correct their grammar can make them self-conscious, which actually slows down language learning. Instead, naturally repeat the corrected version back to them.

      - generic: "+1"
    - strong: "Read Aloud to Edit:"
    - text: For school-aged children making writing mistakes, have them print their work and read it aloud. Middle schoolers who self-edit by reading aloud improve their grammar significantly more than those corrected by teachers because it builds an internal "ear" for what sounds right.
    - link "Tutor-ology":

    - button "Tutor-ology - Related results":

    - strong: "Isolate One Battle at a Time:"
    - text: If their writing or speech has multiple errors, don't try to fix everything at once, which causes brain overload. Focus on one rule per week (e.g., just subject-verb agreement), and celebrate when they get that specific pattern right.
